Big open questions in science, tested in the open.

One person and a team of AI agents trying to solve three famous open problems by 2027, in public, so anyone can check the work or join in.

Zero passed from hand to hand, India to Baghdad to Pisa, and became everyone’s. Science moves fastest when it is shared; these projects share every step. Hover over a picture for its story.

About this site

  • What this is

    A public lab notebook. Agents test ideas on existing data; every result is published, failures too.

  • Who it is for

    Researchers who want to check or reuse the work, and anyone with an AI assistant who wants to help.

  • Why these questions

    Famous, unsolved, testable on open data, and an answer would be clearly right or wrong.

  • The goal

    A checkable result on at least one by 2027. If we fail, everything stays public for the next team.

Agents make the slow part of science cheap

An AI agent is a program, like ChatGPT, that carries out a whole task on its own: it finds the data, writes the code, runs the test and reports back. Big questions rarely stall for lack of ideas; they stall because checking each idea takes people and years. Agents can rerun a test on published data overnight. They can’t run new experiments, so we work with data that already exists.

  1. Fields change when failures pile up

    Kuhn’s The Structure of Scientific Revolutions shows a field shifts only when results it cannot explain become too many to ignore. Agents can test many ideas quickly, and we count every test we run, so a lucky hit can’t pass as a finding and every failure stays on the record.

  2. Discoveries come from mixing experts

    In The Idea Factory, Bell Labs puts physicists, chemists and engineers in the same corridors, and the transistor comes out of it. Agents can draft a chemist’s or a statistician’s checks in minutes; then real experts review them.

  3. Big change can start in a small circle

    In 1760s Birmingham about a dozen friends, among them Watt, Wedgwood and Erasmus Darwin, met each full moon to share experiments; the moon lit their ride home. Their circle, told in The Lunar Men, helped start the Industrial Revolution. Ours is people and agents, and the seats are open.

Agents can also fool themselves faster than people can, so every project follows the same rules. The three books are also a short course on running a discovery group: Scientific discovery.

Principles of agentic research

How we run research with agents. The method below is how we judge what they find. Drawn from our handbook on building with agents and three books on how discovery happens.

  1. Aim at problems nobody would staff. Agents give a small team more workers than ideas. If they run out of work, the goal is too small.

    From Building with agents, ch. 7

  2. Read before you run. Open the closest papers first. If what is new cannot be said in one sentence, don’t run the study.
  3. Try to kill the idea first. Run the cheapest test that could end it before building the full study. Most ideas should die in an afternoon.
  4. Start the day the idea appears. No backlog. Give each test to an agent right away, keep several running at once, and let a coordinator agent steer them.

    From Building with agents, ch. 1 and 3

  5. Start over from scratch now and then. Give a fresh agent the goal but not our history, and compare its plan with ours. It shows the routes we never tried and the work we kept only because we had started it.
  6. Borrow from other fields. Have agents read the latest work in neighbouring fields and ask what would transfer. Bell Labs got the transistor by putting physicists, chemists and engineers in one corridor.

    From The Idea Factory

  7. Count every failure. Fields move when unexplained results pile up, so every null goes on the public record with the effect it could have caught.

    From Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions

  8. Don’t trust an agent’s confidence. Agents sound as sure when wrong as when right. Check every finding and every citation before acting on it.

    From Building with agents, ch. 5

  9. Turn what works into a skill. When a method works, write it down as instructions any agent can load, so the next study starts from the best one.

    From Building with agents, ch. 4

  10. Document everything in the open. Plans, code, data, dead ends and corrections go public as they happen, so anyone can check the work, reuse it or tell us where it is wrong. The Lunar Society shared its experiments in letters; we share ours on GitHub.

    From The Lunar Men

  11. People keep the last word. Agents do the work. A person chooses the goals, judges the results, and approves anything that goes out to the world.

    From Building with agents, conclusion

Which projects

One method for every project

A result that looks good must not be something you could get by trying until something works. These rules are the same in every project, and every result can be rerun from its code.

  1. Seal it before you look. Every prediction, test and pass mark is written down and given a digital fingerprint that is published before any result is seen, so it cannot be quietly changed later.
  2. Test on data it never saw. Part of the data is held back, and near-copies of it never reach the people building the idea.
  3. Plant an answer first. We hide an answer we already know in practice data. If a method cannot find it there, we do not trust what it says about the real data.
  4. Let someone else try to break it. Every positive result goes to a separate team, of people and agents, whose job is to find the flaw.
  5. Publish it either way. Failures are written up with the size of effect the test could have caught.

Contribute

Each project is run by one person and a team of AI agents, with a public list of open tasks. Anyone can pick one up.

Talk to us first: join the community on Slack. Ask questions, pick a task, or tell us we are wrong.

No coding needed:

  • Tell us where we are wrong about your field. Historians, linguists, clinicians and chemists catch what agents miss.
  • Point us to data we are missing. Each project lists what would change its odds most.
  • Check a result. Each finding says what was tested; tell us if it does not hold up.

If you use an AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT or similar), give it an open task. Each project has a ready-made prompt per task: Open Mind, Open Origins, Open Indus. It writes down its plan, checks it can find a planted answer, runs the test and sends the result back to us, whichever way it goes.
